Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 237-2 Filed 03/02/26 Page 2 of 17 Christopher Williams, PhD Professor of Pharmacology Chair, Division of Basic Pharmaceutical Science Xavier University Pharmacy Annex 425 November 17, 2025 Chip Wagar, Esq. Wagar Hickman LLC 1401 W. Causeway Approach Mandeville, LA 70471 Re: Pharmacological Opinion: Death of Harmony Moller Kathleen Moller v. Martian Sales, Inc. et al. Dear Mr. Wagar: I have been requested to provide expert opinion in the case of Kathleen Moller vs. Martian Sales, Inc., et al. I hold a PhD in Pharmacology (Tulane University) and over 20 years of experience in molecular pharmacology research and instruction. Specifically, I have been engaged in pharmacy education in pharmacology since 2009 at Xavier University of Louisiana, where I currently serve as the chair of the Division of Basic Pharmaceutical Sciences and as an endowed chair in pharmacy. My research program in mechanisms of drug action has been consistently funded through National Institutes of Health and foundation grants throughout my tenure. I have mentored over 25 PharmD, MS, and undergraduate students in the pharmaceutical sciences, many of whom went on to expand their expertise in medical, graduate, and postdoctoral training opportunities. Regarding my independent expertise in pharmaco-legal matters, I function under PharmCognitive Consulting, LLC and have consulted in at least 9 cases, of which one proceeded to trial. My goal in this case is not to identify cause of death, nor is it to provide clinical diagnostic information. Rather, my role is to provide the scientific background on the pharmacological activity of Kratom (mitragyna speciosa) alkaloids, and the mechanistic underpinnings of its drug-like effects when consumed or utilized as a so-called nutritional supplement or food. My opinions herein are given to a reasonable degree of scientific certainty. Harmony Moller, the plaintiff’s daughter, was found unresponsive in her home, and later declared deceased, after consuming Kratom, evidenced by the presence of Kratom

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 237-2 Filed 03/02/26 Page 3 of 17 packaging on the scene and autopsy reports detecting mitragynine (MG) in collected blood samples. The cause of death was officially documented as “abnormally high left coronary ostia takeoff exacerbated by mitragynine use”. It is my opinion that the mechanisms of Kratom alkaloid activity support this conclusion, and I agree with the findings of Dr. Thundiyil and Dr. Wharton in this regard. Kratom, or Mitragyna speciosa, is a plant species native to Southeast Asia and has been traditionally used as an analgesic and to combat fatigue among laborers and farmers, particularly when either chewed (in leaf form) or steeped as a tea. The species contains several pharmacologically active alkaloids, and as such Kratom has been implicated as both a substance of abuse as well being touted for its’ potential therapeutic applications. Though over 40 alkaloids have been isolated from Kratom, the major constituent is mitragynine (MG), representing over 60% of the alkaloid content in most extracts. Related, 7-hydroxy mitragynine (7HMG) represents a minor component (less than 2%) of the alkaloid content of leaf extracts, but more importantly is generated through hepatic CYP-mediated metabolism of MG once ingested. These Kratom alkaloids exhibit significant opioid-like activity. In experimental models, MG exhibits partial µ opioid receptor agonist activity with approximately 25% relative potency of morphine. Accordingly, MG exhibits naloxone-sensitive antinociceptive properties, providing further evidence that MG indeed functions through opioid-like mechanisms. 7HMG has 10-fold greater potency than morphine and significantly increased latency in response to noxious stimuli in studies of analgesia. Collectively, these studies demonstrate that Kratom contains alkaloids which rival the potency of clinically available opioids like morphine in experimental models1. A third metabolic derivative, mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (MGPI), shows even greater affinity for the µ opioid receptor (80pM range), though the rate of transformation and accumulation in human blood has not been well defined. In addition to their effects on the µ opioid receptor, studies suggest that MG and 7HMG have antagonist functions at the δ and κ opioid receptors. Outside of opioid receptors, MG has demonstrated agonist activity at the α2A adrenergic receptor, which is thought to contribute to its analgesic effects, as well as CNS depressant activity, and antagonist activity at the serotonin (5HT2A) receptors. These findings collectively provide evidence that Kratom derived alkaloid may function to have significant impact on multiple drug receptor systems, while lacking the selective nature of well-defined pharmaceuticals.

Among the most significant opioid-related adverse drug effects is respiratory depression. 7HMG has 4/5 fold greater respiratory depression effect compared to morphine, whereas MG induced a respiratory stimulant activity elicited through its non-opioid actions2. It is important to note that MG is hepatically bio transformed to yield 7HMG and therefore has the potential to produce similar effects as well. Human kinetics suggest that ingestion of dried Kratom leaf preparations lead to a blood ratio of 7HMG:MG of 0.20 to 0.29, even though 7HMG only represents about 1% of the total alkaloid content in Kratom. This would suggest that a significant amount of MG is converted to 7HMG by CYP3A4 after ingestion3. As such, the ingestion of Kratom yields significant amounts of both MG and 7HMG, and subsequently yields pharmacological activity associated with both compounds throughout the duration of exposure. Beyond the respiratory adverse responses, cardiotoxicity has been clearly linked to opioid usage including Kratom, which includes QT prolongation. Experimental models have shown that MG inhibits delayed rectifying K+ currents, similar to methadone, potentially leading to cardiac arrhythmias. It is important to note that blockade of K+ signaling has been implicated in sudden cardiac death related to toxic opioid exposure through increased duration of action potential in cardiac models4. This is reflected in the findings of a 2023 study of the FDA Adverse Events Reporting System (FAERS) which showed that MG was associated with a greater incidence of ventricular arrhythmia/cardiac arrest than any other drug tested, including methadone. In 39% of those cases, MG

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 237-2 Filed 03/02/26 Page 5 of 17 exposure was indicated in the absence of concurrent QTc prolonging drugs, thereby suggesting that MG was the primary driver of cardiotoxicity5. Individual case studies paint a similar picture. In one such published case, an otherwise healthy 25 year old was hospitalized with compromised left ventricular ejection fraction and elevated troponin I levels, with no other confounding substances found upon urinalysis6. The lack of receptor specificity should be noted as well. MG has documented stimulant-like activity, which has been attributed to its ability to modulate adrenergic receptors. Furthermore, Kratom alkaloids may impact the serotonin receptors and dopamine release, each of which can have substantial impacts on cardiovascular function. It is plausible that these actions contribute to the negative impact on cardiovascular status when concomitantly administered with other drugs with cardiovascular stimulant effects. Kratom derived products also sit at the juxtaposition where pharmacologically active so-called nutritional supplements/foods have robust drug effects and therefore are involved in drug-drug interactions. This can lead to unintentional cases of polypharmacy, where drugs with overlapping off-target effects can result in significant toxicity. In the case of Harmony Moller, Kratom may well impact K+ currents in the heart and exacerbate the typically moderate effects of antihistamines like diphenhydramine or promethazine. Of note, the levels of the diphenhydramine (64 ng/ml) and promethazine (18ng/ml) are in accordance with expected levels in therapeutic drug usage, suggesting that these drugs alone were not used at a level that should precipitate cardiorespiratory toxicity (toxicity is apparent near (100ng/ml range for either drug)7. Additionally, the typically benign elevated heart rate that is associated with cannabis use might present another potential unrecognized interaction with Kratom alkaloids. While causality is difficult to ascertain in cases of polypharmacy induced drug effects, the mechanistic underpinnings are present for significant drug-drug interactions involving MG and 7HMG. This report is based on my training and expertise in pharmacology and my assessment of the current consensus in scientific literature. I am being compensated at a rate of $250/hr. for my research and consultation in this case. I have no conflict of interest that would result in bias. I am being reimbursed through Plaintiff’s counsel for the work that I am providing as an expert on an hourly basis. I am not employed by any company that dispenses or promotes the use of kratom. I never met Harmony Moller, nor do I know the Moller family. I reserve the right to rephrase or alter my opinions as additional information is received. I reserve the right to supplement this report when further data, documents, or

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 237-2 Filed 03/02/26 Page 8 of 17 Assistant Professor, 02/2009-09/2015 Tenure Track Faculty: As faculty in the COP, my primary teaching responsibilities include instruction in pharmacology across various therapeutic areas within the curriculum. Additionally, I have had the opportunity to participate in ACPE self-study and accreditation site visits. I have served on the university research committee, faculty association executive board, faculty representative for the board trustees, AACP delegate, Academic Affairs Council, and the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee. Additionally, I have been integrally involved in the development of a new PharmD curriculum which emphasized the vertical and horizontal integration of core therapeutic areas in pharmacology, medicinal chemistry, and pharmacotherapeutics. Chair, Division of Basic Pharmaceutical Sciences: As Chair of Basic Pharmaceutical Sciences, I provide leadership, oversee the basic science elements of the didactic curriculum, and serve as an advocate for faculty and staff in our division. My primary goal has been to foster a “habit of excellence in teaching, scholarship, and service”, and under my direction the division has made it a priority to provide support for professional development opportunities. In addition to working to support faculty and staff, I collaborate with the chair of clinical sciences to oversee the day-to-day execution of the didactic PharmD curriculum. I am a standing member on the Dean’s Executive, Curriculum Review, Academic Council, Academic Standing, and Program Assessment Committees, each of which provides opportunities to participate in the governance of the College. I have made concerted efforts to increase the educational offering that we have availed to our students. I have led our efforts with LSU Health Sciences Center for a PharmD-PhD bridge program, which allows for the attainment of both PharmD and PhD degrees for students whose interests lie in the area of translational/clinical pharmacology. In addition, I have spearheaded the development of a new MS in Pharmaceutical Sciences, and contributed to the development of our recent MS in Physician Assistant Studies. Most recently, we were recipients of $1M in funding through the National Institute for Innovation in Manufacturing Biopharmaceutical (NIIIMBL), with the goal of training students in te manufacturing of biologics. Currently, I am also overseeing the launch of our COVID19 testing hub for HBCUs in our geographical area and our on campus COVID19 molecular testing laboratory, funded by the Just project (ThermoFisher).I also serve as the Xavier co-director for the Ochsner Xavier Institute for Health Equity and Research (OXIHER), which is supported by $1.2M from the WK Kellogg Foundation. Research: As chair, I have maintained an active research program in breast cancer experimental therapeutics. The three main projects are summarized below: Functional dichotomy of NURR1 in breast cancer etiology and progression- Our laboratory is currently studying the etiological significance of the orphan nuclear receptor NURR1 in breast cancer etiology. These studies center around

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 237-2 Filed 03/02/26 Page 9 of 17 investigating the mechanisms underlying the conditional tumor suppressor function of NURR1, with an ultimate goal of designing pharmacological agents targeting the receptor. Cell-extrinsic effects of metformin in the breast tumor microenvironment- Metformin, the first line anti-diabetic drug, has recently achieved attention as a potential antineoplastic agent. Our lab has shown that metformin impacts the expression of inflammatory intermediates in breast cancer cells. Here, our goal is to determine if metformin can alter the development of chronic inflammatory conditions within the breast tumor microenvironment, and thereby prevent breast tumorigenesis. Successful completion of these studies may support a role for metformin usage as chemo preventive among patients at risk for development of breast cancer. CK2 mediated regulation of estrogen receptor function- CK2 is a ubiquitously expressed kinase which is overexpressed in rapidly proliferating tissues. Our previous studies have shown that CK2 modulates estrogen receptor activity by impacting specific phosphorylation sites in the receptor. We are currently investigating the impact of CK2 on agonist and antagonist sensitivity of estrogen receptor in BCa. Successful completion of these studies may support the role of CK2 as a viable pharmacological target in breast cancer which is refractory to hormonal therapy. Teaching/Instruction: “Pharmacology I and II” “Pharmacology Lab”, “Principles of Drug Action”, “Medicinal Chemistry/Pharmacology I, II, III and IV,” “Pharmacogenomics”. Instructional focus areas include- general pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics, introduction to autonomic physiology/pharmacology, cholinergic drugs, drugs for the treatment of dyslipidemia, drugs for the treatment of anemia, anticoagulant/fibrinolytic drugs, anti-inflammatory drugs, antineoplastic drugs, principles of toxicology. In pharmacogenomics, instructional areas focused on genetic variability in drug targets. With curricular revision, we integrated medicinal chemistry with pharmacology, with the intention of creating more synergy in the context of teaching the two disciplines. This content was also coordinated into the pharmacotherapeutics course series. Tulane School of Medicine, Cancer Center (2004-2008) Postdoctoral Fellow, Department Structural and Cellular Biology, The major focus of our laboratory was the study of nuclear receptor signaling in cancer. We identified novel post-translational regulatory sites in ERα, and assessed their role in cellular signaling in breast cancer. These studies included the characterization of estrogen receptor α crosstalk with growth factor receptor kinase signaling pathways in mediating resistance to therapy in breast cancer. Pilot projects included the study of NR4A orphan nuclear receptor signaling in breast cancer. Our group’s studies focused on the role of ErbB4 tyrosine receptor signaling in breast cancer. We demonstrated that ErbB4 mediates nuclear accumulation of the transcription factor STAT5A, physically

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 237-2 Filed 03/02/26 Page 10 of 17 associates with an endogenous STAT5A responsive promoter, and is required for ErbB4-mediated transcriptional activation of STAT5A. These studies were the first to show that ErbB4 acts as a transcriptional coactivator in breast cancer. Additionally, our lab identified novel serine residues in STAT5A which are phosphorylated in response to ErbB4. Mutation of these serine residues abrogates STAT5A transcriptional activity in response to ErbB4. In addition we studied the regulation of estrogen receptor transcriptional activation in a process requiring ErbB4 cleavage and nuclear localization.
